title: The 1925 Italian Hall benefit dance with Paul's band
summary: Mares recalls a 1925 benefit dance for Battling Barreau at the Italian Hall, the band lineup, and the repertoire they played.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Let me interrupt about that picture in your other office. It's the poster, rather. I noticed it was dated up here at the Italian Hall at 1925. Do you know who played that dance?
Yes, that was a benefit for battling Barreau. Paul had Santo and Rapp.
Rapp was still... Oh, Rapp, yeah, Rapp played.

That was in 1925. And they were playing around New Orleans as a unit at that time. But of course, George Brunner stayed in Chicago and Santo Pacora took his place. And we had Leo Addy, one of the real great drummers of that time on drums. And we had Charlie Cadela playing tenor sax. And we had Freddie Newman played piano and Red Long. Both of them played with the outfit. And this particular date, Freddie Newman was playing.
You remember the dance in particular? Oh, yeah. You were there, no doubt.
Yeah, it was at the Italian Hall right here on Esplanade and Rapport, 1925.
It says 75 cents admission. We'll get a copy, a photo, a picture of that some of these days.
Well, that's an old collector's item deal there.
Anything about the dance you can remember, for instance, how they played? They played great.
Oh, yeah. They played all the old numbers like Millen Boyg and Tin Roof Blues and Zero, all those popular numbers.
Did they play many things like ordinary pop tunes, you know, or waltzes or anything? Oh, yeah.

They played the waltzes in Swanee River, old Kentucky home, all that with the beat in it, naturally. Anything that anybody came that thought they'd like to hear, they played it and naturally put the old Rhythm King's beat to it. It was a great band and it done a lot of good for Battlin' Barrella. And the band was really clicking that day because they weren't dancing. They were standing in front of the bandstand. And any time you see that, Bill, that they don't want to dance and listen to the different musicians play, well, then you know that they're playing.
